cards.b: Training matched to the activity, muscles and fitness component needed. A sprinter does sprints.
Gradually increasing the work so the body keeps adapting.
Fitness gained is lost when training stops or is reduced.
Boredom from repeating the same training, which lowers motivation.
Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard), Time (how long), Type (kind of training).
About 60–80% of max heart rate. Improves cardiovascular endurance.
About 80–90% of max heart rate. Improves speed, power and lactic acid tolerance.
Steady pace without rest for 20+ minutes. Improves cardiovascular endurance.
Continuous running with unplanned changes of speed and terrain. Trains aerobic and anaerobic fitness.
Work periods alternating with rest periods. Improves speed and anaerobic capacity.

short.q: Calculate 70% of the maximum heart rate for a 14-year-old.
Explain how progressive overload could be applied to a weight-training programme.
short.model: Gradually increase the weight, reps or sets over the weeks. This keeps challenging the muscles so strength keeps improving.

short.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of circuit training.
short.model: Advantage: many people can train at once and stations can suit the sport. Disadvantage: needs space and equipment, and technique can slip when tired.

short.q: Which training method is best for a sprinter wanting to improve speed, and why?
short.model: Interval training, with short fast sprints and rest. It is specific to sprinting and trains the anaerobic system.

short.q: Describe the three seasons of training and what happens in each.
short.model: Pre-season builds a fitness base and sport-specific fitness. Competition season maintains fitness and sharpens skills. Off-season gives active rest and recovery from injury.
